narrative:
The model determined that you have a 60.5% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability exceeds the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile is far below the average of accepted students (around the middle of the class), signaling that your later academic performance raised significant concerns about your readiness for the bar.

Your LSAT score of 33.5 worked in the opposite direction, pulling the prediction toward passing. While helpful, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the other factors.

Your first-year class ranking came in third in importance and again pushed the outcome toward failure. Like your third-year standing, being in the lowest decile placed you well below the typical accepted student, who ranks near the middle of their class.

Taken together, these academic signals outweighed your solid family background, full-time study plans, and other details.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on raising your academic performance and retake the LSAT if possible. Strengthening these two areas will directly address the factors that led to this rejection and improve your chances in a future application. (218 words)
